passage: In the support room of a ticketing software company, Santosh read a public post from a user, Sabina: the export button had wiped her saved filters twice, and no one had answered. The team gathered round Santosh's screen. Nobody wanted to argue. Santosh wrote the reply and the others checked it: 'Thank you for telling us, Sabina, and sorry about the lost filters. It's a bug on our side. A fix goes out on Thursday, and we'll post here when it's live.' On Thursday the fix went out, and Santosh wrote a second public reply confirming it and offering help to restore her filters. Sabina answered, 'Faster than I expected, thanks.' Two other users who had grumbled in the thread added thumbs-up.

qa.q: When did the fix go out?
qa.a: The fix went out on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel after the second reply?
qa.a: Sabina felt pleased and a little surprised, shown by 'Faster than I expected, thanks.'

qa.q: What could the team add to catch complaints like this sooner?
qa.a: The team could assign someone to watch public posts every day, so problems get an answer the same day.

qa.q: How might the two grumbling users have seen the exchange?
qa.a: They likely saw a team that listens and follows through, and adding thumbs-up suggests their view had softened.

grounding: Shows a team replying politely, thanking the user, saying what will be fixed and by when, then following up publicly after the fix.

passage:
Dear Usha,
Thank you for posting about the booking error on our app. You were right: when you changed your travel date, the app charged you twice, and our support team took four days to answer. That shouldn't have happened, and I'm sorry.
Here is what we are doing. The double charge has been refunded; you should see it in your account within five working days. Our engineers found the bug in the date-change screen and will fix it in the update on 18 July. And we are adding weekend support staff from this month, so no one waits four days again.
I'll post here again after the update goes live, so you and others can check.
Gurpreet, for the team

19 July: The fix is live. Thank you, Usha, for helping us find it.

qa.q: When will the bug be fixed?
How might Usha feel reading this reply?
qa.a: Usha is likely to feel heard and relieved, since the reply admits the mistake, refunds the double charge and names a fix date.

qa.q: Why is posting again after the fix a strong step?
qa.a: It shows the promise was kept in public, which can turn critics into supporters and reassure others who saw the complaint.

qa.q: How might other users who saw Usha's post see the team now?
qa.a: They see a team that admits mistakes and follows through, which can build more trust than if nothing had gone wrong.

grounding: It shows a team thanking a critic, explaining what will be fixed and by when, and following up publicly after the fix.

passage: Maria, you asked on your show how a small company handles angry customers online. Here's what we learnt. I'm Minakshi, and I run support for a food delivery startup in Indore. Last winter a customer posted that our app kept cancelling his orders at dinner time. Four hundred people agreed in the replies. We didn't argue. Within an hour I replied: 'Thank you for flagging this. We see it too. Our team is testing a fix, and we'll update this post by Friday.' On Friday we fixed it, and I went back to the same post and wrote: 'Fixed. Please tell us if it happens again.' The same man replied, 'Respect.' Some of the people who complained became our loudest supporters. It wasn't magic. We just said thank you, said what we'd fix, and then actually did it.

qa.q: By when did Minakshi promise to update the post?
How did Minakshi feel when the man replied 'Respect'?
qa.a: Minakshi likely felt proud and relieved, seeing a critic turn friendly after the promise was kept.

qa.q: What else could Minakshi's team do after the fix?
qa.a: They could look for similar dinner-time problems before customers notice, and keep replying the same way to new complaints.

qa.q: How might the customer who complained see the company now?
qa.a: He felt heard and saw the fix happen, so he went from angry to respectful.

grounding: It shows a team thanking a critic, explaining what will be fixed and by when, and following up publicly after the fix, turning critics into supporters.
